statement: The organization's mission and business context, including the services it delivers, are documented and approved by leadership. Security risk priorities are tied to the mission or to those services in the risk strategy and in risk decisions. This keeps security effort aimed at what the business depends on. Proof is the approved mission statement, the risk strategy and a risk register extract.
why_asked: Without a link to the mission, security priorities drift toward what is easy or fashionable and the board cannot see why risks rank as they do.
how_to_ask: Ask for the approved mission or purpose statement, then ask how the risk priorities connect to it. Look for a named business service on the risk entries. Example probe: "Take your top risk. Which service or mission objective does it threaten, and where is that written down?"
question: Does your organization tie its security risk priorities to a leadership-approved statement of its mission and key services?
expected_evidence: Approved mission, vision or purpose statement with approval record; security risk strategy or methodology; risk register extract showing the mission objective or service each risk affects; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: A written mission statement carries leadership approval. The risk strategy states that priorities follow the mission or the services that deliver it. Recent risk decisions record which objective or service each risk affects.
test: Obtain the mission statement and the risk strategy. Check the mission is approved by leadership and the strategy ties risk priorities to the mission or services. Sample three risk decisions from the period and check each names the objective or service affected. Pass if all three hold.
baseline_risk: Security spending and risk rankings are disconnected from what the business needs, so critical services stay under-protected.

statement: The risk direction, the risk method, security roles and planned risk responses are delivered to the people who must act on them. Each item is sent by a defined channel when it is issued or changed. Proof of receipt is kept, such as distribution lists, acknowledgements or briefing records, and role holders confirm they understand their roles.
why_asked: Risk direction that was written but never delivered is not followed, and an auditor needs proof that the people deciding and acting actually received it.
how_to_ask: Pick one artifact, such as the risk method, and ask how the people who apply it got it. Ask for the record of delivery. Example probe: "Show me how the last change to the risk rating method reached the risk owners, and who confirmed they understood it."
question: Does your organization make sure the people who act on its risk direction, methods and roles have received them?
expected_evidence: Distribution records or briefing sign-in sheets for the risk strategy and risk method; role appointment letters or signed acknowledgements; job descriptions stating security duties; risk reports sent to owners and leadership; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: Each artifact has a named audience and a delivery record. Role holders have been told their security roles and confirm them. Planned risk responses reach the affected stakeholders. Follow-up exists when duties were not met. Sub-asks: risk response direction to decision makers, risk method to its users, roles to role holders, planned responses to stakeholders.
test: Obtain the delivery records for the risk direction, risk method, role assignments and risk responses. Sample three role holders and three risk owners and check each has a record of receipt in the period. Pass if every sampled person has a dated record for each item that applies to them.
baseline_risk: Decision makers and role holders act on outdated or unknown direction, so risk is accepted or ignored inconsistently.

statement: A program of security tests and exercises, such as penetration tests, tabletop exercises and recovery tests, is planned and scheduled, and includes critical suppliers and relevant third parties where it matters. Each test or exercise produces a report that records the improvements identified. Each improvement has an owner and is tracked to closure. Proof is the plan, the reports and the action tracker.
why_asked: Tests that are ad hoc, skip key suppliers or leave no tracked actions do not make the organization better prepared.
how_to_ask: Ask for the test and exercise plan, then the reports from the last cycle. Check actions have owners. Ask whether a critical supplier took part. Example probe: "Show me the last exercise report, the actions it raised and where a supplier was involved."
question: Does your organization run a planned program of security tests and exercises, recording the improvements each one identifies?
expected_evidence: Security test and exercise plan or schedule; penetration test, tabletop and recovery test reports; improvement action tracker with owners and status; record of supplier involvement or reason for none; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: A schedule covers the main test types. Reports state the improvements found. Every improvement has an owner and a status. At least one test or exercise involved a critical supplier, or a record explains why none was needed.
test: Obtain the plan and the reports for the period. Sample three improvement actions and check each has an owner and a tracked status. Check at least one exercise involved a critical supplier or records why not. Pass if the plan exists, reports record improvements and all sampled actions are tracked.
baseline_risk: Weaknesses in people, process and supplier links stay hidden until a real incident exposes them.
